newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine analysts, officials cheer Letes results.
newsitem.headline: Argentine analysts, officials cheer Letes results.

text.p: Argentine officials and analysts cheered yields that were dramatically below expectations and very heavy bidding at today's Letes Treasury bill auction.
"It was a truly excellent result. It is the best result in volume as well as in rate terms," Miguel Kiguel, Argentina's undersecretary of finance, told Reuters.
The Economy Ministry auctioned 250 million pesos of 91-day Treasury bills at a discount strike rate of 6.10 percent and $250 million of 182-day bills at 6.09 percent.
Both issues had been expected to come in at around 6.50 percent -- 40 basis points above the actual results.
What is more, bid-to-cover ratios of 5.33 on the 91-day bills and 8.65 on the 182-day bills showed a huge amount of demand for the bills, analysts said.
"This is yet more evidence of the very high levels of liquidity in the system," said Hugo Diaz Lourenco, senior analyst at consultancy C&E Consultores.
The Argentine bond market has been buoyed for a while by high foreign capital inflows, which had been expected to help today's auction as well.

The 6.10 percent rate on 91-day peso bills was the second lowest recorded since the government introduced the current monthly Letes auction program at the beginning of last year. The lowest was in May 1996 when there was a rate of 5.70 percent.
Last month's sale of 91-day peso bills drew a rate of 6.40 percent.
The rate on the 182-day dollar bills, meanwhile, was the lowest recorded since the Letes were introduced.

The "6.10 percent is a seriously low rate, although one has to remember there was one lower rate in May last year, when there was a rate of 5.7 percent," said Hernan Hircks, an economist at consultants Broda y Asociados. "We knew the auction would be successful, just not this successful.
"The internal market is very liquid and the Letes are a good investment," added Hircks.
Kiguel said the result also showed the Letes program is maturing.
"I think the system is fully up and running now and it is very positive. The most important thing is that it is strengthening the capital markets," he said.
"Both Argentine banks as well as foreign ones now know that the domestic market is the most important vehicle for the Letes placements. They also know the importance of being market makers."
The system was first introduced with a view to building up the domestic debt market under an organized market-maker system.

Officials hoped it would attract more funds to the domestic market and in time extend the maturity of the instruments sold locally. Recently Bonte Treasury bonds with maturities of up to two years have been added to the system.
"There is an incredible liquidity level. There is an impressive boom in the market," said the chief bond trader at a Argentine bank.
